blocks.html: Consistency is used in many contexts with different meanings. These notes gives an overview of these definitions and are recommended to gain clarity.

blocks.html: Data Consistency
blocks.text: Data Consistency

blocks.html: Data Consistency means that clients see same data, with strictness or relaxations applied as needed based on system requirements and feasibility.
blocks.text: Data Consistency means that clients see same data, with strictness or relaxations applied as needed based on system requirements and feasibility.

blocks.html: In distributed systems, data is usually replicated across multiple nodes to improve availability, fault tolerance, and latency.
blocks.text: In distributed systems, data is usually replicated across multiple nodes to improve availability, fault tolerance, and latency.

blocks.html: However, this replication introduces a challenge: keeping all replicas in sync.
blocks.text: However, this replication introduces a challenge: keeping all replicas in sync.

blocks.html: Because of network delays or faults, updates may reach replicas at different times.
blocks.text: Because of network delays or faults, updates may reach replicas at different times.

blocks.html: As a result, two clients querying different nodes may see different values temporarily.
blocks.text: As a result, two clients querying different nodes may see different values temporarily.

blocks.html: These temporary inconsistencies cannot be completely avoided in a replicated system.
blocks.text: These temporary inconsistencies cannot be completely avoided in a replicated system.

blocks.html: To manage them, systems adopt different consistency models.
blocks.text: To manage them, systems adopt different consistency models.

blocks.html: Each model defines rules for when updates become visible across replicas.
blocks.text: Each model defines rules for when updates become visible across replicas.

blocks.html: No model is universally best — each comes with trade-offs between consistency, availability, performance, and complexity.
blocks.text: No model is universally best — each comes with trade-offs between consistency, availability, performance, and complexity.

blocks.html: Consistency in distributed systems is not absolute but exists on a spectrum, with different models offering varying degrees of guarantees about how and when updates are observed.
blocks.text: Consistency in distributed systems is not absolute but exists on a spectrum, with different models offering varying degrees of guarantees about how and when updates are observed.

blocks.html: Consistency vs Correctness
blocks.text: Consistency vs Correctness

blocks.html: Data Correctness: Means the data itself is logically accurate according to the application rules (e.g., account balance, like counts on a post, timestamp etc should never be negative).
blocks.text: Data Correctness: Means the data itself is logically accurate according to the application rules (e.g., account balance, like counts on a post, timestamp etc should never be negative).

blocks.html: Data Consistency (in distributed systems): Means all replicas agree on the same value (strictly or with relaxations), even if that value is wrong due to a bug.
blocks.text: Data Consistency (in distributed systems): Means all replicas agree on the same value (strictly or with relaxations), even if that value is wrong due to a bug.

blocks.html: Key difference:
blocks.text: Key difference:

blocks.html: A system can be consistent but incorrect (e.g., all replicas show the like count on a post as -10).
blocks.text: A system can be consistent but incorrect (e.g., all replicas show the like count on a post as -10).

blocks.html: A system can be correct but inconsistent (e.g., two replicas show the like count 10 and 20 respectively).
blocks.text: A system can be correct but inconsistent (e.g., two replicas show the like count 10 and 20 respectively).

blocks.html: Correctness is about truth of the data (can it be really true if seen alone in one DB); Consistency is about agreement of the replicas.
blocks.text: Correctness is about truth of the data (can it be really true if seen alone in one DB); Consistency is about agreement of the replicas.
